We investigate several key aspects of LLM performance in Tibetan:

· We evaluate all LLMs on Ti-MMLU and TiSafetyBench, measuring their Tibetan multi-task understanding and safety capabilities.

· We assess the impact of language resource availability by comparing CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and Ti-MMLU and extend this analysis to safety evaluation by comparing SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023） with Ti-SafetyBench.

· We explore the differences between reasoningoptimized LLMs and chat LLMs， examining whether reasoning enhancements improve lowresource language performance.

· We study the effect of LLM size on Tibetan language understanding, comparing different parameter variants of LlaMA-3.1 (Dubey et al., 2024) and Qwen-2.5 (Qwen Team, 2024).

# TLUE: A Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation Benchmark

Fan Gao1,\*, Cheng Huang1,3,4,\*, Nyima Tashi2†, Thupten Tsering1,5,t Yutong $\mathbf { L i u ^ { 1 } }$ , Ban Ma-bao1, Xiangxiang Wang1, Xiao Feng1, Renzeg Duojie² Gadeng Luosang², Rinchen Dongrub², Dorje Tashi², Hao Wang1,6, Yongbin $\mathbf { V } \mathbf { u } ^ { 1 , \dagger }$

lUniversity of Electronic Science and Technology of China, ²Tibet University 3University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center,4Southern Methodist University 5The State Key Laboratory of Tibetan Intelligence,University of Connecticut

Github: https://github.com/Vicentvankor/TLUE \* Equal Contribution, + Corresponding Authors

# Abstract

Large language models have made tremendous progress in recent years,but low-resource languages,like Tibetan, remain significantly underrepresented in their evaluation. Despite Tibetan being spoken by over seven million people, it has largely been neglected in the development and assessment of large language models. To address this gap,we present a Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation Benchmark, TLUE, the first large-scale benchmark for measuring the proficiency of LLMs in the Tibetan language. TLUE comprises two major components:a comprehensive multi-task understanding benchmark spanning 5 domains and 67 subdomains,and a safety benchmark encompassing 7 subdomains.Then,we evaluate a diverse set of state-of-the-art large language models.Experimental results demonstrate that most large language models perform below the random baseline,highlighting the considerable challenges they face in Tibetan language processing. TLUE provides a crucial foundation for advancing future research in Tibetan language understanding and highlights the importance of promoting greater inclusivity in the development of large language models.

# 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) have made significant strides in natural language understanding, excelling in high-resource languages like English and Chinese through extensive datasets,advanced architectures, and benchmarks like GLUE (Wang et al., 2018) and SuperGLUE (Wang et al., 2019). However, many mainstream LLMs, like GPT(OpenAI, 2024; Achiam et al., 2023), Claude (Anthropic, 2024), Gemini (DeepMind, 2024), LlaMA (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen (Qwen Team, 2024) and DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025,2024) largely overlook low-resource languages, such as Tibetan, which limits the inclusivity and fairness of AI systems and restricts their applicability to underserved language communities (Bender et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). For Tibetan, it is one of the languages included, spoken by over seven million people,which has unique grammatical features and limited annotated data (National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2021). Despite its cultural importance, Tibetan is underrepresented in current LLM research and benchmarks (An, 2023; Liu et al., 2025a, 2024).

Current language understanding benchmarks, in

ple,which has unique grammatical features and limited annotated data (National Bureau of Statistics of China, 2021). Despite its cultural importance, Tibetan is underrepresented in current LLM research and benchmarks (An, 2023; Liu et al., 2025a, 2024).

Current language understanding benchmarks, including GLUE (Wang et al.， 2018)， SuperGLUE (Wang et al., 2019), and BIG-bench (Srivastava et al., 2O22), focus on high-resource languages, leaving low-resource languages like Tibetan without tailored evaluation frameworks, including benchmarks from China (Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). Even existing methods do not adequately capture Tibetan's linguistic intricacies (Liu et al., 2022; Lv et al., 2025). So, in this paper, we introduce the TLUE, a Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark, the frst large-scale benchmark for Tibetan, designed to address the unique challenges of low-resource language evaluation. Furthermore,we selected several state-of-the-art LLMs for training and evaluation,and the experimental results demonstrate that TLUE effectively exposes the limitations of current models in handling Tibetan language tasks. Most LLMs show significantly lower performance on TLUE compared to benchmarks in high-resource languages, particularly struggling with tasks requiring deep linguistic understanding and domainspecific knowledge. This highlights the urgent need for more inclusive pretraining data and architecture adaptations tailored to low-resource languages like Tibetan. Our findings validate TLUE as a robust tool for evaluating and guiding the development of more equitable language models.

All in all, the main contributions of our work are summarized as follows:

· We developed and publicly released TLUE, the first large-scale Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark. It is designed to fill the gap in existing resources by providing a comprehensive suite of tasks that span 67 knowledge-based subdomains and 7 safety-critical categories,addressing both general understanding and ethical alignment in Tibetan.

· We evaluated several state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-4o(Achiam et al., 2023) and GPT-O1-mini (OpenAI, 2024), Claude-3.5- Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024), Gemini-1.5 (DeepMind, 2024), LlaMA-3.1 (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen-2.5 (Qwen Team, 2024), DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al.， 2024) and DeepSeekR1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), to systematically assess their capabilities in both general Tibetan language understanding and safetyoriented tasks. These LLMs represent a diverse set of architectures and training strategies,enabling a broad comparison of their performance under low-resource conditions.

· Our qualitative and quantitative analyses reveal substantial limitations in current LLMs when applied to Tibetan. Most models performed significantly below expected baselines, even falling below random choice levels on certain tasks, particularly in domains requiring complex reasoning or cultural sensitivity. These findings underscore the urgent need for research into more inclusive, linguisticallyaware model development tailored to lowresource languages.

# 2Related Work

# 2.1 Language Understanding Benchmark

LLMs have been extensively evaluated on multilingual and domain-specific benchmarks, such as XTREME (Hu et al., 202O), XGLUE (Liang et al., 202O), and MASSIVE (FitzGerald et al., 2022). However, these benchmarks predominantly focus on high-resource languages, with little attention given to low-resource languages like Tibetan. CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2O23) introduced large-scale Chinese language evaluations,but no equivalent benchmark existed for Tibetan.

# 2.2 Low Resource Language Evaluation

Several efforts have been made to extend LLM evaluation to low-resource languages. IndicGLUE (Kakwani et al., 202O), and INDICGENBENCH (Singh et al., 2O24) focus on Indic languages, while projects such as AmericasNLP (Mager et al., 2021) and Masakhane (Nekoto et al., 2O2O) target indigenous and African languages. Despite these advances, Tibetan remains significantly underrepresented in LLM evaluation.

# 2.3Safety and Ethical Limitations in LLM

Recent work has also examined the safety and ethical risks of LLMs,particularly in multilingual and low-resource contexts. Studies such as SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2O23) and HolisticEval (Liang et al.,2023） assess biases,fairness,and robustness in AI systems.However, these benchmarks largely exclude Tibetan and other low-resource languages, leaving significant gaps in understanding how safety concerns manifest in such linguistic environments.

# 2.4Motivation

Based on the current progress of LLM in minority languages,we propose the TLUE, filling the gap by providing a comprehensive Tibetan evaluation dataset across multiple domains and safety-related tasks.We referred to the two benchmarks, CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2O23), and asked Tibetan language experts to manually translate and verify them. In summary, the combination of Ti-MMLU and TiSafetyBench forms TLUE. TLUE can not only enable systematic evaluation of model performance in a challenging low-resource setting, but also introduces a dedicated safety evaluation suite for Tibetan, providing insights into model robustness and potential vulnerabilities in a low-resource language context.

By offering a comprehensive,multi-domain framework for both language understanding and safety evaluation,TLUE fills a critical gap in the current landscape of LLM benchmarks,enabling systematic assessment of Tibetan language models in a challenging low-resource setting.

# 3TLUE

In designing TLUE,we adhere to several key principles to ensure a rigorous and meaningful evaluation of TibetanLLMs.

First, we align our benchmark with existing multilingual evaluation frameworks to facilitate direct comparison with established benchmarks. This allows researchers to assess the performance of Tibetan LLMs relative to models trained in other languages, providing a broader perspective on crosslingual capabilities (Park et al., 2024).

Additionally, we ensure that the evaluation data is carefully curated and free from data leakage, maintaining the integrity of benchmark results and preventing unintended memorization effects (Doe and Smith, 2024).

# 3.1 Curation Process

As shown in Figure 1, the TLUE benchmark follows a structured multi-stage process to ensure the quality and cultural relevance of Tibetan evaluation data in the curation process. Source datasets, such as CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023), are first translated into Tibetan using Claude-3.5-Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024) , which demonstrates strong Tibetan text generation capabilities. The translations undergo rule-based filtering to correct syntactic inconsistencies and structural errors.

Following this, human annotators, including 2 Tibetan language specialists and a team of 5 additional annotators, refine the dataset to preserve linguistic accuracy and classical Tibetan grammar. Annotators are compensated at an hourly rate of 28 USD,ensuring high-quality review and incentivizing skilled professionals.

The final phase includes domain-specific validation,where legal, medical, and scientific content is reviewed by subject-matter experts for accuracy. This multi-layered curation approach ensures TLUE remains a comprehensive and culturally adapted benchmark for Tibetan language model evaluation.

# 3.2Size

TLUE consists of 22,963 evaluation questions, divided into Ti-MMLU for knowledge assessment and Ti-SafetyBench for safety evaluation.

Ti-MMLU includes 11,528 multiple-choice questions across 67 subjects, covering social sciences, STEM, China-specific topics,humanities, and other domains, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of Tibetan language understanding. TiSafetyBench contains 11,435 questions across 7 safety categories,including ethics,bias, health,and privacy, designed to assess LLMs’ ability to handle sensitive content.

While Ti-MMLU focuses on broad,multidomain knowledge evaluation, Ti-SafetyBench targets high-precision safety assessments, together forming a balanced and comprehensive Tibetan language benchmark. The dataset sizes are summarized in Appendix A Figure 5,which i

# 3.3Why Extend Existing Benchmarks?

Developing a benchmark for Tibetan presents challenges such as limited annotated corpora and linguistic expertise. TLUE extends existing benchmarks via translation, enhanced with human annotation and quality control. Key reasons include:

· Enabling Cross-Lingual Comparability: a translation-based benchmark provides parallel data to compare Tibetan model performance across languages, isolating linguistic effects from task knowledge.

· Addressing Data Scarcity and Leveraging Established Designs: due to limited Tibetan corpora, TLUE adapts reliable,pre-validated benchmarks like CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023),ensuring task diversity and alignment with Tibetan's linguistic and cultural traits.

·Ensuring Quality through Controlled

Adaptation: TLUE uses a multi-stage adaptation process (translation, filtering,alignment, annotation) to balance efficiency with linguistic precision,maintaining high benchmark standards. This structured approach provides a high-quality, scalable framework for assessing LLM performance in Tibetan, especially in low-resource settings.

# 4Implementation

Our experiments cover a diverse range of LLMs, including both open-source and proprietary LLMs:

· Open-source LLM: we evaluate several opensource LLMs,including LlaMA-3.1-405B (Dubey et al., 2024), LlaMA-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen-2.5-72B (Qwen Team, 2024)，DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024), and DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al.. 2025). These LLMs represent a Variety of architectures and parameter scales, allowing for a broad comparison of open-source advancements in Tibetan language understanding.

· Proprietary LLM: we also evaluate several proprietary LLMs, including GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024), GPT-3.5-Turbo (Achiam et al., 2023), Claude-3.5-Sonnet (Anthropic,2024), Gemini-1.5-Flash-Latest (DeepMind, 2024), and O1-Mini (OpenAI, 2024). These models serve as strong baselines forcommercialLLM performance in Tibetan tasks.

# 4.1 Experimental Setup

We investigate several key aspects of LLM performance in Tibetan:

· We evaluate all LLMs on Ti-MMLU and TiSafetyBench, measuring their Tibetan multi-task understanding and safety capabilities.

· We assess the impact of language resource availability by comparing CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and Ti-MMLU and extend this analysis to safety evaluation by comparing SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023） with Ti-SafetyBench.

· We explore the differences between rea

understanding and safety capabilities. · We assess the impact of language resource availability by comparing CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) and Ti-MMLU and extend this analysis to safety evaluation by comparing SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2023） with Ti-SafetyBench. · We explore the differences between reasoningoptimized LLMs and chat LLMs， examining whether reasoning enhancements improve lowresource language performance. · We study the effect of LLM size on Tibetan language understanding, comparing different parameter variants of LlaMA-3.1 (Dubey et al., 2024) and Qwen-2.5 (Qwen Team, 2024). # 4.2Evaluation # 4.2.1Evaluation Methodology We employ zero-shot evaluation to simulate realworld conditions where LLMs must perform tasks without task-specific examples, providing a more accurate assessment of performance in Tibetan. Appendix Figure 7 illustrates the TLUE prompt format and example queries used in evaluation. To ensure consistency, we use the default temperature settings for each model during inference,avoiding bias from manual adjustments. # 4.2.2Evaluation Metrics We evaluate LLMs’ performance on TLUE using two metrics: Response Rate, Accuracy and Conditional Accuracy. · Response Rate measures the proportion of valid responses. · Accuracy tracks the proportion of correct answers. · Conditional Accuracy reflects the LLM's performance when giving valid responses. For both Ti-MMLU and Ti-SafetyBench, We use two methods for metric calculation: · Direct Answer Calculation measures if the LLM selects a valid and correct answer. · Concern All Answer Calculation evaluates the LLM's maximum performance by considering all valid options and selecting correct answers based on remaining choices. # 6Conclusion

This paper presents TLUE,a benchmark for evaluating large language models in Tibetan, covering general knowledge understanding(Ti-MMLU) and safety alignment (Ti-SafetyBench). We show that both proprietary and open-source models struggle in Tibetan, performing below or near the random baseline. We identify key challenges, including significant performance drops when transitioning from high-resource languages to Tibetan, limitations in current multilingual training,and the need for enhanced Tibetan language resources. While opensource models show promising domain-specific improvements, reasoning-optimized models demonstrate better generalization but face difficulties in following Tibetan prompts. Model scaling provides inconsistent benefits,with architecture, data quality, and fine-tuning strategies proving more crucial than model size.These results underscore the need for improved pretraining and targeted fine-tuning, with TLUE serving as a foundation for future lowresource language modeling research, promoting inclusivity and robustness in LLM development.

# AAppendix: Details of TLUE

As shown in Figure 5, $\mathbf { T L U E } ^ { 1 }$ consists of 2 subbenchmarks: Ti-MMLU and Ti-SafetyBench. Together, these two components offer a comprehensive evaluation of both the general knowledge proficiency and safety alignment of LLMs in Tibetan. TLUE emphasizes challenges unique to low-resource languages and supports zero-shot and few-shot settings to facilitate cross-model comparisons without relying on language-specific tuning.

# A.1Ti-MMLU

Ti-MMLU² is an evaluation sub-benchmark designed specifically for Tibetan LLMs,similar to MMLU (Hendrycks et al.,202O) in the English field and CMMLU (Li et al., 2023) in the Chinese field.It comprehensively tests the LLM's knowledge understanding and reasoning capabilities in a multi-disciplinary and multi-task environment through multiple-choice questions.

As shown in Figure 6, Ti-MMLU contains 67 subtasks,covering multiple subject areas from middle school to university and even professional examinations, such as mathematics,physics,history, law, medicine, engineering, philosophy, literature, etc., covering the unique local knowledge system in Tibetan areas, such as college entrance examinations, teacher qualification certificates,medical examinations, etc.,and is particularly suitable for evaluating the LLM's mastery of Tibetan language context and professional knowledge.

Ti-MMLU uses zero-shot or few-shot settings, does not provide contextual learning,and directly examines the generality and true capabilities of the model.
